fetched_contents.text: Time-to-digital converter Device in signal processing In electronic instrumentation and signal processing, a time-to-digital converter (TDC) or time digitizer (TD) is a device for recognizing events and providing a digital representation of the time they occurred. For example, a TDC might output the time of arrival for each incoming pulse. Some applications wish to measure the time interval between two events rather than some notion of an absolute time, and the digitizer is then used to measure a time interval and convert it into digital (binary) output. In some cases,[1] an interpolating TDC is also called a time counter (TC). When TDCs are used to determine the time interval between two signal pulses (known as start and stop pulse), measurement is started and stopped when the rising or falling edge of a signal pulse crosses a set threshold. This pattern is seen in many physical experiments, like time-of-flight and lifetime measurements in atomic and high energy physics, experiments that involve laser ranging and electronic research involving the testing of integrated circuits and high-speed data transfer.[1] Several methods exist for time digitization. Some types allow for nanosecond accuracy, while other are capable of picosecond accuracy (see Coarse measurement and Fine measurement sections below, respectively). Application TDCs are used to timestamp events and measure time differences between events, especially where picosecond precision and high accuracy is required, such as the measurement of events in high energy physics experiments, where particles (e.g. electrons, photons, and ions) are detected. Another application is cost-effective and non-mechanical water flow metering by measuring the time difference between ultrasound pulses that travel through the flow and arrive at different times depending on the flow speed and direction.[2][3] In an all-digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL), a TDC measures the phase shift and its result is used to adjust the digital controlled oscillator (DCO).[4] Coarse measurement If the required time resolution is not high (nanosecond resolution?), then counters can be used to make the conversion. Basic counter In its simplest implementation, a TDC is a counter that increments every clock cycle. At any particular moment, the contents of the counter indicates the current time. When an event occurs, the counter's value is captured in an output register. In this approach, the measurement is an integer number of clock cycles, so the measurement is quantized to a clock period. To get finer resolution, a faster clock is needed. The accuracy of the measurement depends upon the stability of the clock frequency. Typically a TDC uses a crystal oscillator reference frequency to achieve good long term stability. High stability crystal oscillators are usually relatively low frequency, such as 10 MHz (or 100 ns resolution).[5] To obtain higher resolution, a phase-locked loop frequency multiplier is sometimes used to generate a faster clock. For example, the above crystal reference oscillator might be multiplied by 100 to get a clock rate of 1 GHz (1 ns resolution). Counter technology High clock rates impose additional design constraints on the counter: if the clock period is short, it is difficult to update the count. Binary counters, for example, need a fast carry architecture because they essentially add one to the previous counter value. A solution is using a hybrid counter architecture. A Johnson counter, for example, is a fast non-binary counter. It can be used to count very quickly the low order count; a more conventional binary counter can be used to accumulate the high order count. The fast counter is sometime called a prescaler. The speed of counters fabricated in CMOS-technology is limited by the capacitance between the gate and the channel and by the resistance of the channel and the signal traces. The product of both is the cut-off-frequency. Modern chip technology allows multiple metal layers and therefore coils with a large number of windings to be inserted into the chip. This allows designers to peak the device for a specific frequency, which may lie above the cut-off-frequency of the original transistor. A peaked variant of the Johnson counter is the traveling-wave counter which also achieves sub-cycle resolution. Other methods to achieve sub-cycle resolution include analog-to-digital converters and vernier Johnson counters. Measuring a time interval In most situations, the user does not want to just capture an absolute time that an event occurs, but wants to measure a time interval, i.e the time between a start event and a stop event. That can be done by measuring an arbitrary time of both the start and stop events and subtracting. The measurement can be off by two counts. The subtraction can be avoided if the counter is held at zero until the start event, counts during the interval, and then stops counting after the stop event. Introduction Electromyography (EMG) is a widely used method that records the electrical activity of muscles by measuring the electrical potential created when a muscle contracts (voluntarily or not). EMG signals can be detected directly using invasive electrodes placed in the muscle or as a superposition of signals gathered using electrodes applied at the surface of the skin. In the latter technique, known as the surface electromyography (sEMG), the signal is the combined electrical activity created by all motor units. When EMG was first developed, only intramuscular electrodes were used. However, inserting electrodes is an invasive procedure and implanted electrodes cause patient discomfort during muscle movement; sEMG was introduced to overcome these problems [1]. sEMG has several advantages over the use of invasive electrodes. In Proceedings of the 20th IEEE International NEWCAS Conference, Québec City, QC, Canada, 19–22 June 2022. Submission received: 23 January 2023 / Revised: 13 February 2023 / Accepted: 28 February 2023 / Published: 3 March 2023 Abstract In this paper, two of the most common calibration methods of synchronous TDCs, which are the bin-by-bin calibration and the average-bin-width calibration, are first presented and compared. Then, an innovative new robust calibration method for asynchronous TDCs is proposed and evaluated. Simulation results showed that: (i) For a synchronous TDC, the bin-by-bin calibration, applied to a histogram, does not improve the TDC’s differential non-linearity (DNL); nevertheless, it improves its Integral Non-Linearity (INL), whereas the average-bin-width calibration significantly improves both the DNL and the INL. (ii) For an asynchronous TDC, the DNL can be improved up to 10 times by applying the bin–by-bin calibration, whereas the proposed method is almost independent of the non-linearity of the TDC and can improve the DNL up to 100 times. The simulation results were confirmed by experiments carried out using real TDCs implemented on a Cyclone V SoC-FPGA. For an asynchronous TDC, the proposed calibration method is 10 times better than the bin-by-bin method in terms of the DNL improvement. 1. Introduction The role of a TDC is to measure precise time intervals between two events represented by two signals (reference and measured signals) [1,2,3,4], which is the keystone of many applications such as LIDAR applications [5], time-resolved fluorescence measurement [6], fluorescence lifetime imaging [7], 3-D active imaging and time-correlated photon counting [8]. In general, high-resolution TDCs can be built as Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) [9]. However, for many applications, it can be better to implement the TDC on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) due to the flexibility and reconfigurability, as well as the short development time of these circuits [10,11,12]. Moreover, the integration of hard processor systems in System-on-Chip FPGA (SoC-FPGA) kits allows performing an on-chip downstream processing such as a post-calibration process [11]. The Coarse–Fine architecture is extensively used to build FPGA-based TDCs to provide a high resolution and a large dynamic range [13,14,15]. The coarse TDC defines the TDC’s dynamic range; it is generally a classical counter clocked by the global system’s clock, whereas the fine TDC, which defines the resolution, is commonly based on the time interpolation technique [16]. The most common structure to build an FPGA-based fine TDC is the Tapped Delay Line (TDL) [14,17]. TDCs can be classified into two main categories: synchronous and asynchronous TDCs. In the synchronous TDC, the reference signal is synchronous with the system clock, and this type of TDCs consists of a coarse and a fine TDC. In contrast, in asynchronous TDCs, both the reference and the measured signals are asynchronous with the clock; thus, these TDCs include a coarse and two fine TDCs, for example, double-TDL. Generally, TDL-based TDCs implemented in FPGA suffer from a large non-linearity due to the large variations in the delay of the TDL cells [18]. This crucial drawback imposes calibrating the TDC to improve the linearity. The most prevailing calibration methods are the average-bin-width and the bin-by-bin methods [1,19,20]. In recent years, many studies have addressed these two methods, especially the bin-by-bin calibration. Nevertheless, most of these works have used this method for the calibration of individual time interval measurement, such as single-shot measurement and averaged measurement, without covering the calibration of histograms, which is an essential procedure for many TDC-based applications. In previous works [21,22,23], time measurement standard deviations of about 18 ps (0.4 LSB), 12.2 ps (1.07 LSB) and 9 ps (0.34 LSB) were achieved, respectively, through bin-by-bin calibration. However, these works did not apply this calibration method to histogram measurements. Furthermore, most of the studies about TDC calibration have predominantly focused on synchronous TDCs [24,25], and very few of them have discussed asynchronous TDCs. The aim of this paper is twofold: (i) to present the methodology and to compare the performance of the aforementioned methods when applied to histograms in the case of synchronous TDCs, and (ii) to propose an innovative robust calibration method for asynchronous TDCs named the “Matrix calibration”. This method, previously presented in [26], is performed as a post-processing of raw data for either ASIC- or FPGA-based TDCs. For its evaluation, this method is compared to the bin-by-bin method which is usually adopted for the calibration of asynchronous TDCs [27]. This paper starts with an introduction about Coarse–Fine TDCs. Section 2 covers the general functional principle of a Coarse–Fine synchronous TDC as well as its most used calibration methods. Section 3 firstly introduces the operating principal and calibration methods of asynchronous TDCs, then presents our proposed calibration method named the “Matrix calibration” in depth. The simulation and experimental results for the calibration of synchronous and asynchronous TDCs are, respectively, presented in Section 4 and Section 5. Padua Quantum Technologies Research Center, Università degli Studi di Padova, via Gradenigo 6B, IT-35131 Padova, Italy Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN) – sezione di Padova, Italy (June 3, 2024) Abstract Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) are a crucial tool in a wide array of fields, in particular for quantum communication, where time taggers performance can severely affect the quality of the entire application. Nowadays, FPGA-based TDCs present a viable alternative to ASIC ones, once the nonlinear behaviour due to the intrinsic nature of the device is properly mitigated. To compensate said nonlinearities, a calibration procedure is required, usually based on an interpolation methods. Here we present the design and the demonstration of a TDC that is FPGA-based and showing a residual jitter of 27 ps, that is scalable for multichannel operation. The application in Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is discussed with a unique calibration method based on the exploitation of single-photon detection that does not require to stop the data acquisition or to use any interpolation methods, thus increasing accuracy and removing data loss. The calibration was tested in a relevant environment, investigating the device behaviour between 5°C and 80°C. Moreover, our design is capable of continuously streaming up to 12 Mevents/s for up to ∼similar-to\sim∼1 week without the TDC overflowing. I Introduction Time-to-digital converters (TDCs) are used in a wide range of applications [1, 2] where picosecond resolution is needed for time detection, such as high-energy particle physics [3], light detection and ranging (LiDAR) [4], quantum communications [5, 6, 7] and quantum random number generation [8]. Recently, Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) have emerged as a popular platform for implementing TDCs due to their flexibility, high-speed performance, and cost-effectiveness [9, 10, 11, 12]. However, standard FPGA-based TDCs require periodic calibration to maintain accuracy, which requires either interpolation methods or stopping the data acquisition process, leading to potential data loss and reduced efficiency [13]. Although it is possible to optimize and automatize the calibration procedure [14, 15, 16], to the best of our knowledge, there are no proposals to overcome the data losses. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allow two parties (Alice and Bob) to create a shared, secret key. To do so, Alice encodes the information in degrees of freedom of a given quantum system, usually photons [17]. To make the sharing of the key successful, Bob requires precise timing of arrival of photons to synchronize both parties effectively, and to allow better distinguishability between signal and noise. For example, algorithms like Qubit4Sync allow Bob to reconstruct Alice’s clock signal from his own qubit measurements [18]. Moreover, QKD is currently evolving to be implemented using satellite links to increase the distance achievable with this protocols [19]. This implies that communication could only be done while the satellite passes through the ground station’s field of view. During this limited time, Bob should receive as much data as possible while maintaining its performance, implying that both calibrating or losing calibration mid-measurement can considerably hinder key generation. In this work, we propose an FPGA-based TDC, named MARTY and implemented on a Zynq7020, that addresses the calibration challenge by integrating a so-called steady calibration111We chose the term “steady calibration” as the terms “self-calibration”, “automatic calibration” or “real-time calibration” are standard forms to indicate just an online calibration procedure which usually include a phase of data loss. method, implemented by exploiting single-photon detection, similarly to what is done in [20] but in a different application framework. This method allows the TDC to calibrate itself using the data it acquires, eliminating the need to stop the acquisition process. This feature not only enhances the efficiency of the system, but also improves the overall time accuracy as each measurement is also a contribution to calibration and there is no distinction between “data-acquisition” and “calibration” phases. The paper has the following structure: in Section II we present the working principle of the system, including the FPGA design, normal and steady calibration procedures, and finally how we performed temperature variation tests on the device; in section III we present the results obtained in this work, including a QKD test performed with MARTY; eventually, in section IV we present the final conclusions and future perspectives. node_outputs.N8:
Traditional electronic readout methods for time-to-digital conversion (TDC) and time-amplitude conversion (TAC) are designed to measure time intervals between events and convert them into digital outputs. A TDC essentially captures the time of an event or the time interval between a start and stop signal, and it can be implemented as a counter that increments with each clock cycle, with the measurement result quantized to a clock period [N1-F1]. More sophisticated TDCs use a coarse–fine architecture, where the coarse part defines the dynamic range and the fine part improves resolution through interpolation techniques like a tapped delay line (TDL) [N4-F3]. In the context of timing readout, TDCs are used to measure precise time intervals between two events, and they are central to applications such as time-of-flight measurements, LIDAR, fluorescence lifetime imaging, and time-correlated photon counting [N4-F3]. The TAC approach, by contrast, maps a time interval into an analog voltage level, which can then be digitized or used directly in subsequent processing [N2-R1].

The basic principle of these methods is therefore simple: a circuit captures the timing of events and converts them into a digital or analog representation that can be processed further. For TDCs, that usually means counting clock cycles between events and then using calibration or interpolation to refine the result [N1-F1][N4-F3]. For TACs, the time interval is converted into an analog amplitude that can be read out as a voltage [N2-R1]. In both cases, the goal is to preserve timing information and make it usable downstream.

Traditional methods struggle with several error sources that are hard to correct with hardware alone. First, clock jitter and quantization error limit the precision of counter-based measurements because the result is tied to the stability of the reference clock and the alignment of the event edges relative to the clock pulses [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Second, nonlinearity is a major issue in TDCs, especially in FPGA-based fine TDCs that rely on TDLs, where variations in delay across TDL cells can create large nonlinearity [N4-F3]. Third, offset and gain errors can distort the digital output of the converter, and ADCs are well known to have these kinds of errors, with self-calibration or internal calibration functions used to correct them [N4-R3]. Fourth, baseline drift and environmental effects can shift the apparent signal baseline, which matters for timing and amplitude measurements because it can mimic or mask true changes in the signal [N3-R3][N3-R5]. The evidence also shows that ambient temperature drifts and device aging can lead to fluctuating baselines that eventually saturate the amplifier chain, which is a classic problem in low-noise, high-speed readout [N3-R5].

The places where timing and amplitude correction are most sensitive to circuit limitations are therefore the same places where the core TDC/TAC design is weakest. Timing correction is most sensitive to jitter, clock stability, and nonlinearity, because these directly affect how precisely the time interval is measured [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Amplitude correction is most sensitive to baseline drift, gain, and offset, because these can shift the apparent signal level without changing the true physical quantity [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, traditional electronics can do a lot, but when the circuit itself has jitter, nonlinearity, offset/gain mismatch, or baseline drift, the downstream correction task becomes much harder and less reliable.
node_outputs.N9:
Hardware-specific calibration in timing readout aims to improve the accuracy and consistency of TDC measurements by addressing specific error sources that are embedded in the circuit design. The evidence points to two of the most common calibration methods for synchronous TDCs: bin-by-bin calibration and average-bin-width calibration [N4-R2][N4-R3]. In addition, the evidence also identifies bin-by-bin calibration as a common method used for asynchronous TDCs and notes that it can be extended to histogram measurements [N4-R2][N4-F3]. For asynchronous TDCs, the paper also proposes an innovative “Matrix calibration” method that improves differential nonlinearity (DNL) substantially and is more robust than bin-by-bin calibration in some cases [N4-F3]. These methods are not generic “signal correction” approaches; they are explicitly TDC calibration techniques designed to correct the nonlinearities, offset, and baseline issues that arise in timing measurements [N4-F3].

Common calibration techniques and what they correct are therefore largely tied to the structure of the TDC. Bin-by-bin calibration is used to improve INL in synchronous TDCs and can improve DNL in asynchronous TDCs [N4-F3]. Average-bin-width calibration also improves DNL and INL in synchronous TDCs [N4-F3]. The paper also notes that TDC calibration is often performed as post-processing of raw data, which implies that calibration can be applied after the initial measurement to refine the timing result [N4-F3]. In the ADC context, offset and gain calibration functions are similarly used to correct the digitized signal by adjusting for systematic offset and scaling errors [N4-R3]. The broader calibration literature also emphasizes that the ultimate objective is to minimize ADC errors and heighten the accuracy of the digitized signal [N4-R1].

Calibration can reduce jitter, offset, gain, and baseline drift, but it does so within the constraints of the hardware architecture. The evidence specifically connects jitter to the clock and to the TDC architecture: jitter on the clock can directly deteriorate the precision of time measurements, and for some DLLs, jitter larger than two time bins can be problematic [N5-R4]. Calibration therefore helps by reducing the effective jitter in the measurement chain, but it cannot eliminate the hardware-dependent jitter source itself. Offset and gain calibration functions are directly aimed at correcting offset and gain errors in the ADC chain [N4-R3]. Baseline drift, though not explicitly tied to TDC calibration in the evidence provided, is a well-known error source in signal chains that can be reduced by calibration and compensation techniques, as seen in the broader signal-processing context [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In timing readout, the evidence suggests that calibration can improve linearity, reduce INL, and improve DNL, but it does not remove the fundamental hardware limitations that cause those errors in the first place [N4-F3].

The practical limits and trade-offs of calibration-only approaches are therefore important. First, calibration is often applied after the measurement is taken, which means it can be a post-processing step rather than an intrinsic part of the readout architecture [N4-F3]. Second, bin-by-bin calibration can improve INL in synchronous TDCs but does not improve DNL, while average-bin-width calibration improves both DNL and INL [N4-F3]. Third, for asynchronous TDCs, bin-by-bin calibration can improve DNL up to 10 times, but the proposed Matrix calibration method is much more robust and can improve DNL up to 100 times [N4-F3]. This implies that calibration can be highly effective, but the effectiveness depends on the TDC architecture and the type of nonlinearity present. Fourth, the evidence also shows that calibration may be limited by the need to measure reference points or to collect histogram data, especially for histogram-based calibration [N4-F3]. Finally, calibration may require additional hardware resources such as ADCs, comparators, and memory, and it may not be able to address all sources of error simultaneously [N4-F3][N4-R3]. Overall, hardware-specific calibration can substantially improve timing readout, but it is best viewed as a complementary correction strategy rather than a universal replacement for better circuit design.
node_outputs.N10:
AI/ML methods could contribute to readout correction by learning the relationships between raw timing/amplitude measurements and the corrected outputs, especially where hardware errors or nonlinearities make traditional calibration difficult or incomplete. The evidence indicates that machine learning is already being used in signal processing and timing correction, and that many ML-based timing calibrations use supervised learning with labeled data generated by measuring radiation sources or by acquiring calibration reference signals [N2-R4][N7-R3]. In timing systems, this suggests that AI can be trained to map noisy or corrupted measurements to the true timing or amplitude value, potentially capturing patterns that are hard to model with simple hardware compensation.

The types of neural networks or models suitable for timing/amplitude correction are not explicitly enumerated in the provided evidence, but the evidence supports the idea that supervised learning models are relevant. Supervised learning relies on labeled data and is used in timing calibrations, which implies that neural networks such as feedforward or convolutional models could be viable [N2-R4][N7-R3]. The evidence also supports the broader use of machine learning in signal processing, where ML enhances accuracy, adaptability, and real-time analysis across various applications [N2-R5]. In the timing context, supervised learning appears especially promising because the calibration task can be framed as a regression problem: given a raw measurement, predict the corrected time or amplitude value [N2-R4][N7-R3]. The evidence also suggests that ML can be used to improve adhesive bondline time-of-flight predictions and ToF data denoising, which are closely related to timing correction [N7-R1][N7-R2]. These examples indicate that AI methods can be used to denoise, interpolate, or correct timing measurements in ways that go beyond traditional interpolation and calibration.

How training data and calibration are collected or simulated is another important question. The evidence shows that supervised learning-based timing calibrations generate labeled data by measuring radiation sources or through other calibration reference signals [N2-R4][N7-R3]. This implies that training data can be collected directly from the system under study, using known reference events or calibrated sources. The evidence also suggests that calibration can be performed as part of the data acquisition process, and that some methods can be implemented using single-photon detection or other calibration signals without stopping the data acquisition [N5-F4]. In addition, the ADC-related evidence indicates that offset and gain calibration can be based on two-point or other calibration points, which can be used as part of the training or validation set [N4-R5]. This suggests that AI/ML can be trained on both raw measurement data and on carefully controlled calibration data, allowing the model to generalize to real-world conditions while still benefiting from hardware-specific calibration references [N4-R5][N5-F4].

Trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and hardware complexity are central to whether AI can be practical. The evidence suggests that AI can improve accuracy by capturing complex nonlinearities and error patterns that are difficult to model with fixed hardware correction [N2-R4][N7-R3]. However, AI methods may introduce latency because they require computation and inference, which can be a concern for high-speed readout systems [N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that calibration and compensation techniques are often designed to be hardware-efficient, such as bin-by-bin or average-bin-width calibration, which are relatively lightweight post-processing steps [N4-F3]. In contrast, more complex AI models may require additional memory, processing power, or specialized hardware, increasing complexity [N2-R5]. The evidence further implies that some ML approaches, such as denoising convolutions, can outperform traditional methods on ToF data, but they are still subject to the same hardware and timing constraints [N7-R2]. Overall, AI/ML can contribute to readout correction by improving accuracy, but it is likely to be most effective when combined with hardware calibration and when the model complexity is kept low enough to preserve latency and resource efficiency [N2-R4][N2-R5][N7-R2].

## 1) What traditional electronic readout methods can do, and what they can’t handle

Traditional TDC and TAC methods are designed to measure time intervals between events and convert them into digital outputs. In time-amplitude conversion, a time interval is mapped into an analog voltage level, which can then be digitized or used directly in downstream processing [N2-R1].

The places where these methods are most sensitive to circuit limitations are the same places where timing and amplitude correction are most difficult. Timing correction is most sensitive to jitter and clock stability, because the measurement is tied to the reference clock and can be affected by asynchronous event edges relative to clock pulses [N1-F1][N5-R4]. Amplitude correction is most sensitive to baseline drift, gain, and offset, because those errors shift the apparent signal level without changing the true physical quantity [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, traditional electronics can do a lot, but when the circuit itself has jitter, nonlinearity, offset/gain mismatch, or baseline drift, the downstream correction task becomes much harder and less reliable.

A TDC essentially captures the time of an event or the time interval between a start and stop signal, and it can be implemented as a counter that increments with each clock cycle, with the measurement result quantized to a clock period [N1-F1]. More sophisticated TDCs use a coarse–fine architecture, where the coarse part defines the dynamic range and the fine part improves resolution through interpolation techniques like a tapped delay line (TDL) [N4-F3]. In the context of timing readout, TDCs are used to measure precise time intervals between two events, and they are central to applications such as time-of-flight measurements, LIDAR, fluorescence lifetime imaging, and time-correlated photon counting [N4-F3]. The TAC approach, by contrast, maps a time interval into an analog voltage level, which can then be digitized or used directly in subsequent processing [N2-R1].

The basic principle of these methods is therefore simple: a circuit captures the timing of events and converts them into a digital or analog representation that can be processed further. For TDCs, that usually means counting clock cycles between events and then using calibration or interpolation to refine the result [N1-F1][N4-F3]. For TACs, the time interval is converted into an analog amplitude that can be read out as a voltage [N2-R1]. In both cases, the goal is to preserve timing information and make it usable downstream.

Traditional methods struggle with several error sources that are hard to correct with hardware alone. First, clock jitter and quantization error limit the precision of counter-based measurements because the result is tied to the stability of the reference clock and the alignment of the event edges relative to the clock pulses [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Second, nonlinearity is a major issue in TDCs, especially in FPGA-based fine TDCs that rely on TDLs, where variations in delay across TDL cells can create large nonlinearity [N4-F3]. Third, offset and gain errors can distort the digital output of the converter, and ADCs are well known to have these kinds of errors, with self-calibration or internal calibration functions used to correct them [N4-R3]. Fourth, baseline drift and environmental effects can shift the apparent signal baseline, which matters for timing and amplitude measurements because it can mimic or mask true changes in the signal [N3-R3][N3-R5]. The evidence also shows that ambient temperature drifts and device aging can lead to fluctuating baselines that eventually saturate the amplifier chain, which is a classic problem in low-noise, high-speed readout [N3-R5].

The places where timing and amplitude correction are most sensitive to circuit limitations are therefore the same places where the core TDC/TAC design is weakest. Timing correction is most sensitive to jitter, clock stability, and nonlinearity, because these directly affect how precisely the time interval is measured [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Amplitude correction is most sensitive to baseline drift, gain, and offset, because these can shift the apparent signal level without changing the true physical quantity [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, traditional electronics can do a lot, but when the circuit itself has jitter, nonlinearity, offset/gain mismatch, or baseline drift, the downstream correction task becomes much harder and less reliable.

Hardware-specific calibration in timing readout aims to improve the accuracy and consistency of TDC measurements by addressing specific error sources that are embedded in the circuit design. The evidence points to two of the most common calibration methods for synchronous TDCs: bin-by-bin calibration and average-bin-width calibration [N4-R2][N4-R3]. In addition, the evidence also identifies bin-by-bin calibration as a common method used for asynchronous TDCs and notes that it can be extended to histogram measurements [N4-R2][N4-F3]. For asynchronous TDCs, the paper also proposes an innovative “Matrix calibration” method that improves differential nonlinearity (DNL) substantially and is more robust than bin-by-bin calibration in some cases [N4-F3]. These methods are not generic “signal correction” approaches; they are explicitly TDC calibration techniques designed to correct the nonlinearities, offset, and baseline issues that arise in timing measurements [N4-F3].

Common calibration techniques and what they correct are therefore largely tied to the structure of the TDC. Bin-by-bin calibration is used to improve INL in synchronous TDCs and can improve DNL in asynchronous TDCs [N4-F3]. Average-bin-width calibration also improves DNL and INL in synchronous TDCs [N4-F3]. The paper also notes that TDC calibration is often performed as post-processing of raw data, which implies that calibration can be applied after the initial measurement to refine the timing result [N4-F3]. In the ADC context, offset and gain calibration functions are similarly used to correct the digitized signal by adjusting for systematic offset and scaling errors [N4-R3]. The broader calibration literature also emphasizes that the ultimate objective is to minimize ADC errors and heighten the accuracy of the digitized signal [N4-R1].

Calibration can reduce jitter, offset, gain, and baseline drift, but it does so within the constraints of the hardware architecture. The evidence specifically connects jitter to the clock and to the TDC architecture: jitter on the clock can directly deteriorate the precision of time measurements, and for some DLLs, jitter larger than two time bins can be problematic [N5-R4]. Calibration therefore helps by reducing the effective jitter in the measurement chain, but it cannot eliminate the hardware-dependent jitter source itself. Offset and gain calibration functions are directly aimed at correcting offset and gain errors in the ADC chain [N4-R3]. Baseline drift, though not explicitly tied to TDC calibration in the evidence provided, is a well-known error source in signal chains that can be reduced by calibration and compensation techniques, as seen in the broader signal-processing context [N3-R3][N3-R5]. In timing readout, the evidence suggests that calibration can improve linearity, reduce INL, and improve DNL, but it does not remove the fundamental hardware limitations that cause those errors in the first place [N4-F3].

The practical limits and trade-offs of calibration-only approaches are therefore important. First, calibration is often applied after the measurement is taken, which means it can be a post-processing step rather than an intrinsic part of the readout architecture [N4-F3]. Second, bin-by-bin calibration can improve INL in synchronous TDCs but does not improve DNL, while average-bin-width calibration improves both DNL and INL [N4-F3]. Third, for asynchronous TDCs, bin-by-bin calibration can improve DNL up to 10 times, but the proposed Matrix calibration method is much more robust and can improve DNL up to 100 times [N4-F3]. This implies that calibration can be highly effective, but the effectiveness depends on the TDC architecture and the type of nonlinearity present. Fourth, the evidence also shows that calibration may be limited by the need to measure reference points or to collect histogram data, especially for histogram-based calibration [N4-F3]. Finally, calibration may require additional hardware resources such as ADCs, comparators, and memory, and it may not be able to address all sources of error simultaneously [N4-F3][N4-R3]. Overall, hardware-specific calibration can substantially improve timing readout, but it is best viewed as a complementary correction strategy rather than a universal replacement for better circuit design.

AI can improve performance in timing and amplitude readout, but it does not replace electronics. The evidence shows that clock jitter can directly deteriorate time measurements and that jitter larger than two time bins can be problematic [N5-R4]. Hardware calibration methods such as bin-by-bin and average-bin-width calibration can improve INL and DNL in TDCs, while Matrix calibration for asynchronous TDCs can improve DNL by up to 100 times [N4-F3]. AI can complement this by learning the remaining timing/amplitude distortions that hardware calibration does not fully remove, especially in systems with time-of-flight (TOF) or similar timing-sensitive applications [N2-R4][N7-R3]. In this setting, AI is not replacing the electronics; it is refining the output after the hardware has already captured the signal.

AI may also degrade system behavior or add overhead in some cases. One clear overhead is latency: machine learning requires computation and inference, and that can be a concern for high-speed readout systems [N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that some calibration methods are designed to be lightweight and efficient, such as bin-by-bin or average-bin-width calibration, while more complex AI models may require additional memory, processing power, or specialized hardware [N4-F3][N2-R5]. In timing readout, where jitter, clock stability, and resolution are critical, any added latency can reduce the effective measurement bandwidth or make real-time operation harder [N1-F1][N5-R4]. The types of models suggested by the evidence are not explicitly enumerated, but supervised learning is clearly relevant, and the evidence also supports broader machine learning use in signal processing, where ML enhances accuracy, adaptability, and real-time analysis [N2-R5]. In practice, feedforward or convolutional neural networks are plausible candidates for timing/amplitude correction, especially for denoising, interpolation, or regression tasks [N2-R4][N7-R3]. The evidence also points to related applications, such as improving adhesive bondline time-of-flight predictions and ToF data denoising, where AI outperforms traditional methods on certain tasks [N7-R1][N7-R2]. These examples indicate that AI methods can be used to denoise, interpolate, or correct timing measurements in ways that go beyond simple hardware compensation.

Training data and calibration are collected or simulated using a mix of direct system measurements and controlled calibration signals. Supervised learning-based timing calibrations generate labeled data by measuring radiation sources or acquiring calibration reference signals [N2-R4][N7-R3]. The evidence also suggests that calibration can be performed as part of the data acquisition process, and that some methods can be implemented using single-photon detection or other calibration signals without stopping the data acquisition [N5-F4]. ADC-related evidence further indicates that two-point calibration can be used as part of the training or validation set [N4-R5]. This means AI/ML can be trained on both raw measurement data and carefully controlled calibration data, allowing the model to generalize to real-world conditions while still benefiting from hardware-specific calibration references [N4-R5][N5-F4].

The trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and hardware complexity are central. AI can improve accuracy by capturing complex nonlinearities and error patterns that are difficult to model with fixed hardware correction [N2-R4][N7-R3]. However, AI methods may introduce latency because they require computation and inference, which can be a concern for high-speed readout systems [N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that calibration and compensation techniques are often designed to be hardware-efficient, such as bin-by-bin or average-bin-width calibration, which are relatively lightweight post-processing steps [N4-F3]. In contrast, more complex AI models may require additional memory, processing power, or specialized hardware, increasing complexity [N2-R5]. The evidence further implies that some ML approaches, such as denoising convolutions, can outperform traditional methods on ToF data, but they are still subject to the same hardware and timing constraints [N7-R2]. Overall, AI/ML can contribute to readout correction by improving accuracy, but it is likely to be most effective when combined with hardware calibration and when the model complexity is kept low enough to preserve latency and resource efficiency [N2-R4][N2-R5][N7-R2].

---

## 4) Can AI improve performance or replace electronics?

AI can improve performance, but it does not replace electronics. The evidence suggests that AI/ML methods are most useful where hardware calibration is incomplete, nonlinear, or too slow to apply in real time, and where the system requires adaptation to changing environmental conditions or complex error patterns [N2-R4][N7-R3][N5-F4]. In other words, AI is complementary rather than a universal replacement, because the core timing and amplitude measurement still depends on the electronics and the calibration architecture [N1-F1][N4-F3].

A key case where AI correction is complementary is when the hardware has residual jitter, offset, gain, or nonlinearities that are difficult to eliminate with fixed compensation. The evidence shows that clock jitter can directly deteriorate time measurements, and jitter larger than two time bins can be problematic [N5-R4]. Hardware calibration methods such as bin-by-bin and average-bin-width calibration can improve INL and DNL in TDCs, while Matrix calibration for asynchronous TDCs can improve DNL by up to 100 times [N4-F3]. AI can complement this by learning the remaining timing/amplitude distortions that hardware calibration does not fully remove, especially in systems with time-of-flight (TOF) or similar timing-sensitive applications [N2-R4][N7-R3]. Supervised learning can also be used for timing calibrations by generating labeled data from radiation sources or other reference signals [N2-R4][N7-R3], which fits well with hardware calibration data collected through offset, gain, or two-point calibration techniques [N4-R5]. In this setting, AI is not replacing the electronics; it is refining the output after the hardware has already captured the signal.

AI may also degrade system behavior or add overhead in some cases. One clear overhead is latency: machine learning requires computation and inference, and that can be a concern for high-speed readout systems [N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that some calibration methods are designed to be lightweight and efficient, such as bin-by-bin or average-bin-width calibration, while more complex AI models may require additional memory, processing power, or specialized hardware [N4-F3][N2-R5]. In timing readout, where jitter, clock stability, and resolution are critical, any added latency can reduce the effective measurement bandwidth or make real-time operation harder [N1-F1][N5-R4]. Moreover, the evidence suggests that hardware-specific calibration is often applied as post-processing of raw data, implying that AI-based correction may add another post-processing layer rather than replacing the original calibration chain [N4-F3]. This can increase complexity without necessarily improving the fundamental hardware limits.

The practical limits of AI in low-noise, high-speed readout are therefore significant. First, AI works best when the signal-to-noise ratio is sufficient to train a robust model, but it cannot eliminate the baseline drift, nonlinearity, or jitter that the electronics themselves produce [N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-R4]. Second, high-speed systems require fast inference, and AI models that are too complex may not meet timing constraints [N2-R5]. Third, AI cannot replace the need for stable clocks, good ADC calibration, or proper TDC architecture; it can only correct the remaining errors after the hardware has already captured the measurement [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R4]. The evidence also shows that hardware calibration can already achieve substantial improvements, such as reducing jitter, offset, gain, and baseline drift, and that some methods can improve DNL by more than an order of magnitude [N4-F3][N5-R4]. AI is therefore most valuable in systems where the hardware already provides a strong baseline, but where the final correction step still needs to adapt to small, changing, or nonlinear distortions [N2-R4][N7-R3].

---

## 5) Bottom line

**Yes, AI can improve existing electronic time-amplitude conversion readout, but only in a complementary way.** It is best understood as a correction layer that learns residual errors and adapts to changing conditions, not as a replacement for electronics or calibration [N2-R4][N7-R3][N5-F4]. The strongest evidence supports that AI can improve accuracy, especially where hardware calibration is incomplete or nonlinear, and where systems require adaptation to environmental changes or complex error patterns [N2-R4][N7-R3][N4-F3]. At the same time, AI can add overhead in latency and complexity, and it cannot overcome the fundamental hardware limits that jitter, nonlinearity, offset/gain mismatch, and baseline drift already impose [N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-R4]. In practice, the most promising approach is to combine AI correction with hardware-specific calibration: use calibration to reduce the largest systematic errors, and use AI to refine the remaining distortions in a way that preserves speed and resource efficiency [N4-F3][N2-R5][N5-F4].

So, if your goal is **improvement**, AI is a strong candidate. If your goal is **replacement**, the evidence suggests that electronics remain essential.
